utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. We had a late start. The first delay was caused by technical problems, and then there were other problems, which caused further delay. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there were a few preliminary matters to be raised. Defence first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. First, we want to inform the other party and the Chamber that Exhibit Number D460, MFI'd, and introduced through Witness Trapara was now completed, and we ask your order for the old number, ET 1D08-0858, to be replaced with a completed translation that bears number 1D11-1847.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the only reason why it was not admitted was the lacking translation. There were no other problems. Madam Registrar, the English translation now in e-court may be replaced by 1D11-1847. Thank you, Mr. Lukic for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's hereby then admitted into evidence because the old one was MFI'd and the new English translation removes any obstacle to admission. Admitted therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next one, another matter, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour. Yesterday we saw that the Prosecution inquired about the composition of the witness statement and how it was produced. We want to inform Your Honours that our witnesses do not participate in composing the statement. They give the statement to members of our team. They do not know how that statement is finalized. If the Prosecution wants to inquire how those statements are composed, they should address us. It is our understanding that we include in the statement what we think that should be included, and the Prosecution has the previous statements for cross-examination. We saw many times in this courtroom, specifically when the Prosecution introduced transcripts, that they took out parts from transcript, from testimony, not only from statements. Then we had the opportunity to cross-examine, to read the transcript. If we want to ask something, we can ask the witness. So there is no need to clarify such things with our witnesses. We also do not have work product from the investigators from the Prosecution. So we do not know what they included in their statements. And I think that the work products are not mandatory for disclosure. So I didn't want to object yesterday when this witness was on the stand because I didn't want to raise that issue in front of him. But as -- as of now, I ask the Prosecution if they want to inquire why something is added or left, they can inquire through cross-examination. And that's all what we have as a preliminary matter this morning, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. On the latter point, Mr. Groome, do you want to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour. I think certainly the Prosecution is entitled to explore differences between the statements, including omissions and additions, just as the Defence did. I'm not exactly sure what particular questions Mr. Lukic is objecting to, but may I suggest that he do object and maybe address them in the context of a specific question that's put to the witness. But as far as I'm aware or as far as -- my position is that all the questions we've asked have been proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I say something. The only -- the only little contradiction, Mr. Lukic, in what you are saying, you said at the beginning that if the Prosecution wants to know how your statements are composed ask you and not the witness. But your last sentence says: "... they can inquire through cross-examination. And that's all we have as a preliminary matter this morning." And that's what they did. They inquired through cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They inquired about the parts of the statement they want to inquire. But they cannot inquire with our witnesses how the statement is composed. They do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But differences, of course, they can cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's not an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That clarifies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it may be a bit more complex. Of course, if you ask a witness about a process of composing a statement which they do not know about, then the simple answer would be: I can't tell you. So, therefore, there is no problem. And your comparison with the selection of transcript portions is not the best comparison I could think of. Because, first of all, everything is available. It's clear that it's a selection. And the issue, as far as I understood it, for the Prosecution, may be that, although there are dates of interviews - sometimes three, four days - that result in almost literally the same text as a statement, and I think that that is what triggered some attention. But, again, I fully agree with you that if a witness is asked a question about how a statement was composed, if he doesn't know, his answer cannot be anything else than: I do not know. But, of course, if there are differences with the previous statements, and if the Prosecution thinks that it may have some meaning, they can verify with a witness, either whether the witness didn't say it again or didn't tell you again, that's something which is within the realm of knowledge of the witness; or whether they intentionally left out and, if so, for what reason. I mean, those questions, of course, a witness could answer. And therefore composition of a statement is a bit more of a complex issue than just who wrote down at what moment, what exactly, but also on the basis of what were notes taken. Did you say -- did you repeat this again, you have told it the Karadzic Defence before, et cetera. These are, as far as I can see at this moment, questions a witness can answer. I don't know whether you have any objection to that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All I'm objecting is -- the questions asked about -- posed to the witness how the statement is composed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- because they do not know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I think matters become more or less clear and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if I can just explain why the statements are almost the same. Of course, the same people, the same incidents, the same indictment. Of course, that we had only some additions or omissions. If the -- we are not interested, for example, in detailed functioning of SDS or stuff like that. But if the witness is talking about the same incident, and this witness did yesterday, the same incident he testified previously in the Karadzic case, of course, that we do not change much in that statement. We tried not to change much --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue is whether you change much or whether the witness changes much, it's still a statement of a witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- rather than a copied version of, and, of course, you can ask questions about how the interview developed. All these questions, in my view, are legitimate questions. But I do agree with you, there are questions where the witness couldn't give an answer, and, therefore, the answer would always be: I can't tell you, I don't know. And we keep a close eye on that if such things will happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is then dealt with. There was a preliminary matter also by the Prosecution to be raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yesterday during the court proceedings, there was a copy of the statement with notes on it. The Prosecution has had the opportunity to -- to review that and we would be asking to increase our cross-examination time, if we could respectively request that, for up to 45 minutes. Although I will try to be much more efficient in my examination than the additional 45 minutes but we would need some additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I spoke with my colleague, Weber, this morning, and we do not have any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, when the Chamber left this courtroom yesterday, I said to my colleagues, Oh, I said to the witness that it would be given back after the break, and I noticed that he had not received it yesterday, so I felt that I had not kept a promise. Is the original available to be returned to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have the copy here. And we can provide it back to the -- to the Registry. However, could we see how the examination goes and then decide whether or not it's something that the Chamber may want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless the witness raises the issue himself, that he has not received it back yet --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it is his property and he gave it to you voluntarily and not in a situation -- at least in a situation where he could expect to get the original back. So for one reason or another, that should be done, and if there would be any dispute as to handwriting or, et cetera, and if you for that purpose need the original, you can keep it for the session. If the witness raises the issue, we'll have to deal with it. So we leave it, at this moment, and we expect you -- and we'll first wait for the -- how the examination develops.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maletic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, our apologies that you had to wait for half an hour, but we had some technical problems and some other procedural issues we had to deal with first. But you're now here. I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and Mr. Weber will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maletic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that you had a conversation with Predrag Trapara before your testimony started. Is it correct that you discussed matters related to your testimony with him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an informal conversation, and I only learned the names of those two girls from him. I was aware of the event, but I didn't know their names. He told me the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How did this subject come up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it in such detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You've both -- by the date you gave, it appears you both have been here for -- for over a week. Did you talk with Mr. Trapara on any other occasions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke before he began testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Was that on one occasion or on multiple occasions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a couple of times. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Was this on a daily basis before he testified?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed everything. Life and such. We talked about anything that we could -- that we could think of when we saw each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And my question, just going back to it, related to basically how often you spoke with him between when you arrived in The Hague and before Mr. Trapara's testimony. Can you tell us whether that was every day, a couple of days? Approximately how many times?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. It is an unclear question, causing confusion with the witness. He needs to be asked whether he discussed the case with Trapara or whether they talked about each other's lives, as the witness said. There's a big difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. Mr. Stojanovic, you can object to a question, but you can't tell Mr. Weber what he should have asked. Another matter is that the witness said already that it has been several times. I don't know ... and your last question was: "Can you tell us whether that was every day, a couple of days? Approximately how many times?" Could you be a bit more precise on how many conversations you had with Mr. Trapara? You said: "Perhaps a couple of times." Was it three times, five times, ten times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twice or thrice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that on one day, or was it on more than one day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps in a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you speak with him alone; that is, under four eyes? Or were others present during those conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were together. I spoke to him. I spoke to Pedja because we hadn't seen each other for quite sometime. We talked about each other's families, life, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Pedja is -- is whom? Is that the same person, or is that a third person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Predrag Trapara. It is the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same person. My question was whether you had these conversations under four eyes or whether others were present as well. Was at any moment during such a conversation someone else present who either listened or may have participated in your conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember such details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was ever any of the members of the Defence team present when you had a conversation with Mr. Trapara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One additional question, please. When did you arrive in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 16th, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you spoke with Mr. Trapara, was it at the same location on these different occasions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we spoke in the hotel, in the lobby.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And just so we have a clear record, was that on every occasion that you spoke with him, that you're describing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase. Did you speak with him anywhere else besides the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Well, perhaps we did take a walk because I walked a lot in these days. But I can't remember whether we took any walks together. I don't think so, though. I think I only spoke to him in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You've broadly said that you spoke with Mr. Trapara about a lot of things; everything, I believe, is what you said. Aside from the two girls, did you speak with him about any topic that related to your evidence here, or Mr. Trapara's?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you watch Mr. Trapara's testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no occasion to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you speak with Mr. Trapara at all after his testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we saw each other after his testimony because he was preparing to travel. But that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you saw him after the testimony, did you discuss anything related to his own testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You didn't even ask him something simple, like: How did it go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. We don't share any particular common interests, so there was no reason for me to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Have you seen or communicated with any other people that have either testified already in this case or will be testifying in this case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw some people who had testified and who are yet to testify, but we didn't broach the topic. Because all of us were in different places at the time, and we didn't have much in common.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could just break this up. If you could just please give us the names of the people that you've spoken with.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cvoro. I have already mentioned Predrag Trapara. Slavko Gengo. I don't recall any other names or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I can't recall the names of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. There are possibly others that -- that were present. Do I understand you correctly? Or that you've had conversations with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay here, I saw some of those people. We talked, we learned about each other, we took walks, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have you spoken with Milorad Dzida?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. When I just asked you a second ago about the names, is there any reason that you did not recall that you had spoken with Mr. Dzida?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I couldn't remember, but I spoke to everyone who was here until now. So whoever was here, up until now, I spoke to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was this all at one time or were these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not a clear answer to the question. A minute ago, when asked for names, you said: "I don't remember the names of those with whom I had a conversation." Mr. Weber then asked you, when you said a minute later, that you had a conversation with Dzida, why you didn't remember his name a minute before. Your answer now is, I spoke to all of them, which is not an answer to the question. The question was: Why didn't you remember that specific name, where you seem to remember it one minute later and without any hesitation. Did you speak with Dzida; yes, I did. That's the question. Have you an answer why a minute later you remembered the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I recalled his name. So let me say it again. I talked to all of them. It's just that at that particular moment I couldn't recall his name. So I talked to all of the witnesses thus far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, if I may just clear something on the record. So you did speak to Mile Sladoje? If do you this, you're not recorded. Say it loud -- say in your voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're nodding, it doesn't appear on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you speak with Mile Sladoje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We met. We hadn't met before, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but you spoke. You said you have spoken to all of them. Mile Sladoje was here. Did you speak with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Branko Radan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Dusan Skrba?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Nikola Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then one additional question. You -- did you touch upon the subject of the testimony you were all to give here in this courtroom? Did you talk about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Most of them I only met here, so I talked to them when we were introduced, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if I understand you well, you never discussed testimony to be given or the subject of appearing before this court as a witness. And then, suddenly, at one moment, either your counterpart or you say: By the way, the names of the girls were A and B. And that was not in the framework of any discussion about testifying. It was just -- came out of the blue? You're not discussing testimony, and suddenly he said: By the way, if you wouldn't know the names, these were the names; or you said: Do you remember the names? I have difficulties in understanding how this suddenly comes up if you are speaking with no one about your testimony appearing as a witness. Whereas the main and -- reason for you all to be here is that you were called as witnesses. I would -- if I were in such a situation -- it's not forbidden. It's not in any way forbidden. I would have discussed with those I would meet, because why not? I mean, that's what you're ... could you explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I talked with Predrag Trapara shortly about the case. With others, I did not. Because we were not in the same positions. Predrag Trapara was a member of our battalion. So, in discussion, a short one, about my statement, when I mentioned this, he reminded me of the names of the girls. I was aware of the incident, but I did not know the names. He just told me that he did know them and that was why I noted them, and I had been aware of the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you brought to court a copy of your statement with notes on the -- the back page, or last pages. Could you just tell us what these notes are?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noted something down for myself in case I needed a reminder, and that's it. Probably you were the first that read it but that was something that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were these notes based on your own personal knowledge or the knowledge of anything that you heard or information you received from anyone else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of the things I heard or learned from others and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. If the Prosecution -- we'll go to these notes, and I'd like to discuss them with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 30720. If we could please go to page 10 of the B/C/S and page 1 of the English translation. There's just a single page of translation related to the notes, but it's the full copy of the statement that was brought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see the text on one of the screens before me but not mine. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, these are the notes that you produced yesterday in court. On the page before you to the left, can you confirm that this is your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did you write these notes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These days, when I arrived here, to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were they written all at once or on different occasions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, there appears to be three lines drawn across the paper which appear to divide your notes into four different sections. I'd like to go through each one with you. The first section, the translation that we have available states: "If there were any it is allowed during the war time since there were no conditions, that is the escape. There were no liquidations and therefore such allegation is insignificant. And even if the conditions were met but they weren't, such security vigilance is tolerant during the war." Mr. Maletic, could you just tell us what -- what this is about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about an order, and I'm reacting to it. I think it dated from 1993. I was asked why, when someone approached the first line of the front, if he wouldn't stop and began to flee, why he should be liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. How did this come up that you felt that you needed to take a note about this order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was confronted with it the previous time, when I was a witness in the Karadzic case. That was why I noted it, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was this something that you discussed with other witnesses who appeared?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the second section. It appears -- or it states: "This is absolutely related to the military targets" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we go to the -- this paragraph. The first line in the previous paragraph reads: "... that is the escape." Escape from what? "If there were any it is allowed during the war since there were no conditions, that is the escape." Escape from what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Escape from the separation line that was the forward front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "If there were any ..." What does the "any" stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any escapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is "allowed during the war time"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If someone approaches the forward line, if he doesn't stop or if he begins to flee, such a person shall be liquidated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So "if there were any" relates, rather, to liquidations than to escapes. Because "if there were any, it is allowed during the war time." "Any," then, being to liquidate someone who tries to escape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is fired -- one is supposed to fire at those who are attempting to escape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in this context, if I read the whole of the line, the last few words "that is the escape," makes no sense anymore in this line. Because then it would read "if there were any," that is, firing at people who tried to escape, "it is allowed during the war time, since there were no conditions, that is the escape." It doesn't make sense to me at all, especially not the last couple of words. So, then, again, my question, escape from what, becomes more urgent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Escape from the forward line, to the enemy line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I still have difficulties in understanding it, but I leave it to that at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My problem - if I may just ask a question - is that Judge Orie asked you "if there were any," and he said what is the "any." You said escape, and later you said liquidation. So which is which between those two? If there were any escapes or if there were any liquidations? Seems to make sense if there were any escapes it is allowed during war time since there were no conditions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Liquidation. I interrupted you. Say what you want to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I continue there, and I say there -- "since there were no conditions," that is, the escape, there were no liquidations. And therefore such allegation is insignificant. "And even if the conditions were met but they weren't, such security vigilance is tolerant during the war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was this a justification that you were expecting to provide for allegations of sniping committed by members of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What's the allegations that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will probably reach that section. It's an order of mine, the details of which I cannot remember now. It dates from 1993. That certain -- I can't remember now, but if we reach that part, I will note it for you, and I will tell you what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, as I understand your evidence as of right now, you are saying that you can't remember the nature of the allegations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As I understand the witness, he doesn't remember the order. Your -- he hasn't answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you recall the nature of the allegation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we get to that case, I will probably recall. I cannot remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know the schedule today was a little -- I can take the break if Your Honours would like to go past schedule or I can continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it would be best to take the break now and then to continue in the usual order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I again have to apologise. There was some urgent matters which kept us busy and which we thought would be more quickly resolved than they actually were. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Maletic, I'm going to go on to the second section from the top in these notes. It states: "This is absolutely related to the military targets and that can be justified from the tactical point of view because it is related to the military force from the opposing side. There was no such order, written or verbal, in terms of civilians. There were many enemy points in that area and legitimate military targets." What was this section about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my previous testimony, I was confronted by something that another witness said, that they were given orders to shoot at anything that was moving, which is not correct. So I noted this in case you were to ask me the same thing. I would say that the idea was that it was legitimate to target military targets and that there was never either a written or a verbal order to target civilians but to target enemy targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The section, I believe, concludes that -- with the statement: "Such statements are arbitrary and fabricated. If he made such statement, did he act upon it." What statements are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wonder, actually - this is my opinion - I wonder if he had such an order to shoot at the other side. If he received something like that, did he act in accordance with it. That's what I'm wondering here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is this "he"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. There was a testimony. It was a protected witness, and it was presented to me that he claimed that we ordered that any moving targets on the opposing side should be shot at. And I claim that we never issued any such orders, that civilian targets were to be shot at, but, rather, just the military targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who presented that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was during the previous trial. That's where they presented it to me and so I noted it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I -- of course, the Chamber has no -- has not looked into the Karadzic transcripts and so, therefore, I take it that the parties will be able to identify what the witness is now talking about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was this anything that you discussed with anyone prior to your testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, unless you had any other questions on this section I was going to go to the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can go to the next one. But, of course, the Chamber would -- since it's not in evidence would appreciate if the parties would verify whether and what statement was put to the witness in a previous testimony as he tells us now, whether that happened; and, if so, what statement that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and I leave it to either you, Mr. Stojanovic, or you, Mr. Weber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The next section states: "Pursuant to the decision of the RS Supreme Court in 1992, the status of a volunteer in the RS -- VRS is that the volunteer in the VRS has no attribute of voluntariness but is a legitimate and legal member of the VRS who can join the army voluntarily but as such could not leave the unit without authorisation of the command because he had the same treatment like any other combatant." Same question, Mr. Maletic: What is this about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noted this for myself, and it is with regard to volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Why did you -- why would you make note of volunteers in advance of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a note of mine, a personal note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber is asking you what the relevance of such a note was in this context. And to say: It's my note, and why not? You could have made notes about the Olympic Winter Games as well, but that, of course, is not -- doesn't explain what the relevance for it is. So could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if the Prosecutor were to ask me about volunteers, then I would read out this paragraph to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why about volunteers? Have you been a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why did you deal with -- why did you expect to be asked about volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I expected that, so in case I was asked that, I wanted to know what I would say. I was asked about that in the previous trial so that was why I supposed that the Prosecutor could ask me that here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now I understand that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were there any volunteers in your unit or the units you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were a few volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Since we're on that topic, could you tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose names?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The names of the volunteers that were in your unit.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. I can't remember the names. In my unit, in my company, there were between 100 and 120 men and around 1.000 men in the battalion, so I can't remember the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did Your Honours have any other questions about this section?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution, at this time, tenders 65 ter 30720 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30720 receives number P6540, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6540 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Maletic, I'm now going to through a number of topics with you for the rest of today. Starting when you were the battalion's assistant commander for intelligence and security, did you allow people to freely move around your zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was freedom of movement. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you ever issue orders to deprive individuals of their freedom to move throughout your zone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 30693.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The right answer to the previous question would therefore have been: We allowed but not always. If you order restrictions on it, then the answer "there was freedom of movement" is not a complete answer. Could I remind you that you're not only bound to tell us the truth but even the whole truth. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thanks for your patience, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is an information report you sent to the 4th Company on the 6th of March, 1993. In this document, you indicate that there were three foreign journalists from Australia and Holland on RS territory. You state that these journalists: "Demonstrated unhidden hatred and lack of objectivity where Serbs were concerned. By their writing, footages and reporting, the said persons caused invaluable harm to the Serb people on the international level." Is it correct that these journalists were reporting on the activities and crimes that were being committed by the VRS and you felt this coverage was not objective?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Then what -- how did they lack objectivity, according to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information we received from the brigade command. And then we sent it further down to the level of companies. And then we would forward that; that is to say, information received from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, please listen to my question carefully. What I asked you was: How did these journalists lack objectivity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably -- well, you see here, the mentioned journalists in their work to date demonstrated unhidden hatred and lack of objectivity towards Serbs. That's written here. Therefore, control should be enhanced and if these persons are found, they should be deprived of their freedom of movement and brought into the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, there seems to be a confusion between question and the understanding of the answer. You asked whether the witness felt and what, according to him, was not objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness's answer was: We received these orders and we passed them on. Meaning that the witness may not have developed his own judgement on the objectivity but it was sent to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if we could go to the signature line on this document. It's on the second page, I believe. Or at the bottom. Sir, that's -- that's your signature on this document, is that correct? This is a report from you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, is on that basis, since you are the actual author of this document, what your reference was to the journalists' lack of objectivity, what you did mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received that information from the brigade command, and I sent it on to company level. I rephrased the order, sent it to company level, so I am not familiar with the journalists. I'm only familiar with the information that I passed on. But I compiled this note or, rather, this information and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's understood. You've mentioned this, that the -- that -- well, in this document, you order the 4th Company to immediately deprive the journalists of their freedom of movement and seize their documents, material, and equipment. Did -- did your battalion, after you gave orders like this, carry them out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have this specific case, so we did not bring them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Is it correct that you had the ability to control the movement of individuals throughout your zone of responsibility? You had the ability to issue orders to do such a thing; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not follow the depth of movement. We could not follow anyone. And the journalists were there. This refers to the first line of combat, the actual front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you had the authority to issue orders to restrict the movement of others?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We got that by way of information or orders from the brigade command. I did not have the right to ban movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you -- I'll move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We tender this document into evidence, if we could, please. 65 ter 30693.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30693 receives number P6541, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6541 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that soldiers are prohibited from committing rape? Sir, did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll repeat it since the record might not be clear right now. Is it correct that soldiers are prohibited from committing rape?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's always prohibited, in wartime and in peacetime, to rape.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you ever investigate any soldiers in Grbavica for committing rape?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P346, page 158 of the English translation, and page 160 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, coming up before you will be an entry from General Mladic's notebooks dated 25 March 1993. It's with respect to a meeting between General Mladic and Prime Minister Radomir Lukic. In this entry, and it's a little up from the bottom for you, General Mladic records: "Some soldiers rape even Serbian women (in Grbavica). (Lukic) himself took someone who had done this out of Sarajevo (he wouldn't say his name)." Is it correct that this entry reflects the living conditions that were existing inside of Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying for my own part -- actually, first, when I was company commander in 1992, as for my area of defence, these soldiers did not rape anyone. That is what I am asserting. As for in-depth in Grbavica, I don't know what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this entry is from 1993. You were the assistant commander for security and intelligence for this area in 1993. Are you saying that were not aware of something that General Mladic was aware of and the prime minister of Republika Srpska was also aware of? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to say that that did not happen in my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of soldiers committing rape in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to that you your testimony of not knowing about these rapes lacks credibility. General Mladic and Prime Minister Lukic were aware of these rapes and that you were in a position to know, and here today you are claiming not to. Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that no one from my battalion, that is to say, I don't know of any rapes, and no one from my battalion committed any rapes. That is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did anyone -- did General Mladic or anyone else from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, you know that you are supposed to remain seated, and -- Mr. Stojanovic. No -- no loud speaking, Mr. Mladic. And if you stand up again, you're removed from the courtroom. Let that be clear. And the same is true for any loud speaking on from now. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it then correct that you never received any instruction from a superior command or General Mladic to investigate this information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An investigation was not carried out. I repeat: I did not know and there were no rapes in my battalion. So there was no investigation either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- could I seek clarification. You are again and again repeating "in my battalion." I do understand clearly from your answer that you say that no soldier in your battalion committed rape. Do you have any awareness of soldiers outside your battalion or even non-soldiers committing rapes in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did any Serb women from Grbavica ever make a complaint?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with such information. Maybe some reports were made at the police station, the civilian police station. That was in the depth of the territory, but, believe me, I'm not aware of that. As for everything that happened in depth, it was the civilian police that was in charge, and they were carrying out these tasks, preventing looting, rape, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, just so you know, it's our position that that answer is -- is not correct, that the military authorities would have had the authority over carrying out discipline for soldiers who committed rapes. Do you not agree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem. But I claim that there were no rapes in my battalion. That's what I've been saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next topic. Is it correct that soldiers are prohibited from looting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you ever investigate any soldiers in Grbavica for looting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P357, requesting page 79 of the English and page 80 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, coming up before you will be another entry from General Mladic's notebooks, dated 21 January 1993, from a session with the Supreme Command. In this entry, I'm going to be directing you to the notes under Colonel Kovacevic's name. This entry records Colonel Kovacevic as stating: "He (Colonel Milosevic) is very brave and audacious. He did not cope well at Grbavica because did he not prevent looting and crime ..." Is it correct that your initial brigade commander, then-Colonel Dragomir Milosevic, did not take action to prevent the looting and crime in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were always orders about the prohibition of crime, looting, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It appears from this entry that looting and crime were taking place in Grbavica. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Again, sir, we have General Mladic at a meeting with the Supreme Command, which appears to include President Karadzic, the prime minister again, what appears to be possibly Bogdan Subotic and other high-ranking members. Is it really your evidence that General Mladic and these individuals in these very high positions would know about looting and crime in Grbavica and you who is the assistant commander of security and intelligence for that very area would not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Again, I put it to you that your evidence on this lacks credibility. You were there every day and you were in a position to know, and you are claiming not to. Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that I don't know what happened in depth in Grbavica because it is a large piece of territory. I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It was your zone of responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't solely our zone of responsibility, and it wasn't only our soldiers were there. Grbavica is much bigger than that. There were other soldiers, and there were policemen there. So it wasn't exclusively my zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And I just want to be clear: Are you claiming that with respect to when you were a company commander or also when you were battalion commander -- or assistant commander? Excuse me, sir.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that you never became aware of any soldiers that were committing looting or other crimes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As concerns my unit, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, my question wasn't limited to your unit.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I wasn't familiar with that. I only spoke of my unit. As for the rest, I had no such information or knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just going to pause here for a second. Throughout your statement, you claim to have very detailed information about stuff that is going on on the opposing side of the confrontation line, areas that I imagine you did not actually go to. How is it that you are claiming that you have no knowledge of areas that you were around during the -- the time of the war, that were, in fact, part of your zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interviewed defectors, those who escaped from the other side, and I obtained information in that way. That is why -- how I knew about what was going on on the other side. At least to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What I'm saying to you, sir, is that there seems to be quite a contrast. How is it not -- that you would not know similar information about what is going on on your own side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the depth of our territory, it was in the area of our police. They were taking care of it. They were actually tasked with working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd like to go onto -- is it correct that a military is prohibited from forcing the expulsions of civilians from an area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you ever take any action to -- or with respect to expulsions of civilians from Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Could you reformulate?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you ever participate or become aware of expulsions of civilians from Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of any civilians being forced to leave Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P307.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, coming up before you is a UN CIVPOL occurrence report dated 30 September 1992. It's regarding the expulsion of Muslim civilians from Grbavica. In the second paragraph, this report indicates that the preliminary information confirmed that the expulsion was in progress, and the Muslims were gathering at the Bristol Hotel. It further indicates that the civil affairs unit was unaware of the exact situation at that time. If I could direct you down to the fourth paragraph, which, in the B/C/S, continues onto the next page, the report indicates the civil affairs unit arrived and made a series of observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please have the next page for the witness in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As you read on, the unit was able to confirm that approximately 300 Muslim civilians were expelled by the Serbs from the area of Grbavica. Do you agree that this act, that expelling Muslim -- part of the Muslim population from Grbavica was an act that was prohibited by the rules of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Expulsion is prohibited. As for those who left Grbavica, perhaps it was in agreement with the civilian authorities that they demanded to leave. I don't know about that. You would need to put that question to a representative of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you again claiming that you were not aware of this event?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that I was unaware of this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. This paragraph continues to state information about the Red Cross. It says, and this goes onto the next page in the English: "Red Cross member confirmed that the expelled Muslims travelled to this area by foot using two different bridges, one identified as Vrbanja Most, near the Assembly building, and the other one just behind the hotel." Is it correct that Vrbanja Most was a bridge that was located in your area of responsibility, your zone of responsibility when you were a company commander, that that was one of the borders of your company's zone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I put it to you that your evidence is incredible that 300 individuals would be expelled across the very bridge for which you would be responsible. Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I have a few questions now before the next break about Veselin Vlahovic, also known as Batko, and Zoran Vitkovic, who you discuss in paragraph 39 of your statement. During your Karadzic testimony, this is at page 30878, you stated: "I spoke about Zoran Vitkovic and I said that since at the time I was a soldier, I only know - and I included that in my statement - that there was a group under the command of Zoran Vitkovic and they were headquartered in the building --" And then the transcript cuts off. There's an interpreter's note, then, in the transcript indicating the name of the building was not heard. Could you please tell us the name of the building where this group was headquartered?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Digitron Buje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where is this building located in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain. I don't have a photograph to explain. It is at the foot of some stairs which eventually lead you up to Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. How big was the size of Batko's group that was headquartered in this building?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were these individuals volunteers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I briefly mentioned everything I knew about the group in my statement. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During your -- during your Karadzic testimony, it continues: "They used to go to certain sections of the front line where the Serbian fighters needed assistance because they were under enemy attack. During one such attack by the Muslim forces, Zoran Vitkovic got killed." Do you stand -- stand by this statement today, from your Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say that this group would go to certain sections of the front line where Serbian fighters needed assistance, who are the Serbian fighters you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went to assist wherever Muslims attacked and wherever help was needed. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that this is -- this was help on the front lines where your forces were positioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't come to assist me. They didn't come to lend assistance in the area between one bridge and the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who are the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. I just wanted to find out from you, Witness, when you say "they went to assist whenever Muslims attacked," who were the Muslims attacking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- what positions, what Serb positions? Serb civilian positions or Serb -- what positions were these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do have you in mind this group which came to assist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- the group, that's what you are telling us, the group that you are telling us came to assist. What Serb positions were being attacked? What do you mean by "Serb positions"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wherever it was necessary. If a Serbian line was in danger, they came to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What Serbian line? Just tell me what Serbs were being attacked. What is this Serbian line or this Serb position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a line was established, the group would come to particular parts of that line if there was any need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who established the line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both we and the Muslims established lines. We were on one side, and they were on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say "we," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serb army on one side and the Muslim army on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say "the Serb army," you mean the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would have answered the first question by "VRS lines," then it would have avoided the whole of the confusion. But if I understand you well, if VRS positions, that is, military positions, the Serb -- the Republika Srpska Army positions were attacked by the Muslims, then those volunteers would come to assist against such an attack. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I said was that this group, which existed at the beginning of the war, came to assist. But they did not stand guard like my soldiers. They came to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they came and assisted when an attack was launched in defending the Serb positions, the VRS positions. Is that well understood? I'm not asking about standing guard. I'm coming to assist when an attack took place. To defend the VRS positions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the group commanded by Zoran Vitkovic went wherever necessary, to assist in order to defend VRS positions. In one such attack, Zoran Vitkovic was killed, and the group disbanded. His soldiers went their separate ways. I don't know what then happened with those soldiers. They were simply no longer to be seen. That is what I talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I was talking also about the period in which the group existed. I mean, you can't say much about the activity of a group if it doesn't exist any further. So I think the way in which I summarised it, you did not at least challenge or contradict that. That is, they came, this group, when still in existence, came at times when VRS positions were under attack to assist in defending those positions. That is how I understood your testimony. And unless you have a clear comment on it, then I'm looking at both parties, whether this is how one would reasonably understand this. There's no need to look at the Defence, Mr. Witness. Mr. Maletic, is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's five minutes past 12.00. We'll take a break, Mr. Mladic, so then you have an opportunity to consult with Mr. Stojanovic. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'll take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 25 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you are on your feet. It seems to be the day of the short delays in our start, but let's try next time to be all there in time. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to, in terms of court scheduling, inform the Chamber that I think I'll be approximately another 20 minutes, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, then, in view of the information I have, that is still within the time-limits. There was quite a bit of questioning by the Judges as well. That's okay. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, already an indication as to how much time you'd then need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, Your Honour, my assessment that -- is that I will need ten minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that the next witness should remain standby to start his testimony today. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P353, page 173 of the English, and page 171 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to be looking at another entry from General Mladic's notebooks. This one is from the 16th of June, 1992, and it records a meeting with Colonel Dragomir Milosevic and the other commanders of units in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And if, for the witness, we could please have the next page in the B/C/S. I believe that's where the statement I will be reading is present.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In this entry, Colonel Milosevic is recorded as stating: "Civilians, free people, and soldiers steal. Zoran Vitkovic is the chief of those who steal ..." Is it correct that this is the same Zoran Vitkovic that you are referring to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is the same person. I am not aware of the fact that there may have been two Zoran Vitkovics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, in this entry, Dragomir Milosevic, who is your brigade commander, again, at that time, is aware of Zoran Vitkovic as being the chief of those who steal and that soldiers are also stealing. How is it that you can explain to us that you were not aware of this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained the situation about my unit. I also explained that I basically didn't know Zoran Vitkovic and that he was not a member of my unit, nor was I a member of his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to read you a passage from your Karadzic testimony, and this is regarding the same exact entry that we're looking at right now. The question that was put to you is: "And that's the same Zoran Vitkovic that you referred to in your statement, isn't it, Mr. Maletic?" Your answer: "Yes, yes. I spoke about Zoran Vitkovic and I said that since, at the time I was a soldier, I only know - and I include that in my statement - that there was a group under the command of Zoran Vitkovic and they were headquartered in the building." Do you stand by this evidence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I again put it to you that your evidence is not credible. Here we have General Mladic and the commanders of the brigades of the SRK being aware of this information, and I put it to you it is not credible, your evidence of a person who you discuss, that you were not aware of his proclivity for stealing. Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said everything I knew in my statement. I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please go into private session for the next matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Maletic, were you informed by your superiors about anything related to the use of prisoners for forced labour?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 18 of your statement, you indicate that your superior command informed you about the actions that were against the rules of war. Did they tell you anything about forced labour?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did they tell anything about whether using prisoners of war for dangerous work details is contrary to the rules of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you aware that placing prisoners in life-threatening conditions is prohibited?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Maletic, at this time, I'm going to ask you to watch a video and then I will have a few questions for you. If at any point in time you need to re-see a portion of the video or watch it a second time, just let us know and we'll replay parts of it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any text in it, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There is. We've disseminated the transcripts to the booths. I'm going to be asking Ms. Stewart to please play a portion of Exhibit P81.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's the duration approximately? Because we have to play it twice if there's any spoken text.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: 58 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And it's beginning at time code 1 minute, 49 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, we received everything in English, but I do not know whether the English text was also received in B/C/S by those who are listening to the B/C/S channel. Was B/C/S, was there any translation? I see Mr. Mladic nodding no. Therefore, it will be played again and then I expect B/C/S translation to be on the earphones of those who are listening to the B/C/S channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we were a bit confused by some of the Defence team members nodding that there had been translation but Mr. Mladic nodding that he had not received it. Let's play it again. And if you could give us further information about time-frame, et cetera, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This came in through Mr. Van Lynden's evidence and I can look up additional information for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He is speaking himself, at least that's what I heard but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- he doesn't say what year or what month or what --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to be asking the witness further questions about his awareness and knowledge after the clip is played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Let's play it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "At Kula that doesn't happen, but the men are forced to work in fields close to Sarajevo's battlegrounds. Some are being hit out in the open, but more have suffered according to the prisoners when they're taken to dig trenches in Sarajevo's front lines, in complete contradiction of all war conventions." "They take us in teams of ten to dig trenches between front line buildings. Usually three dig and three others throw out the earth. It's dangerous. One prisoner has been killed and two wounded. "The Serb warden promises the men will be released if an exchange can be arranged. But none of them are likely to ever be able to return to their home village, now firmly in Serb hands. "Aernout van Lynden, Sky News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could just confirm with the witness that he actually received some type of translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I listened to the B/C/S channel and there was a clear translation on there and same for the French, so there's no -- you've heard it in your own language, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before going into what we just saw, is it correct that your battalion used prisoners from the Kula KPD to perform labour on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rarely, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Is it correct that you personally were involved with the use of prisoners from the Kula KPD?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We just heard some comments of prisoners who were from the Kula KPD. This is from an international broadcast. Were you aware of these allegations at any time during the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution now please have --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So you never saw any type of broadcast like the one that we just saw during your time as a company commander or as an assistant commander in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MALETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please go to 65 ter 3068 -- sorry, 30686.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before -- before we continue, how did you learn about occasionally using prisoners to perform labour on the front lines? How did you learn that, if it was not from Sky News, which I can understand, but how did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a document here in front of me which I signed. It's a report on the escape of two prisoners. They worked in the area of our battalion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd asked you how you learned about it. Do you say it was at this occasion that you learned about it? Because I didn't refer to any document in my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was aware of this document because I signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll wait first for the questions further to be put by Mr. Weber and then see whether there are any remaining questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have -- I have a few questions. You -- you were the commander of your battalion, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
